questions.question: What is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
questions.title: localStorage versus sessionStorage
questions.direct_answer: Both APIs store string key-value pairs for an origin. localStorage persists across browser restarts and is shared by same-origin tabs, while sessionStorage belongs to an origin within one top-level tab and is cleared when that page session ends.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Web Storage scope, lifetime, and data model.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling sessionStorage a server session or assuming it is shared between ordinary tabs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Both APIs are synchronous, can be unavailable or cleared, and are inappropriate for secrets or large structured data.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Both store string keys and values for an origin.
localStorage persists and is shared across same-origin tabs.
sessionStorage is separated by origin and top-level tab.
Both are synchronous and should not hold secrets or large datasets.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` are browser Web Storage APIs that expose string key-value data for an origin. They share methods such as `setItem`, `getItem`, `removeItem`, and `clear`, but their lifetime and browsing-context scope differ.

- localStorage normally survives closing and reopening the browser and is visible to other same-origin tabs. sessionStorage belongs to an origin inside one top-level tab, survives reloads in that tab, and is cleared when the page session ends.

- For example, a colour theme that should remain on the next visit can fit localStorage. A multi-step form draft that should stay isolated to one tab can fit sessionStorage.

- Neither API is a protected vault. Same-origin JavaScript can read the data, users can clear it, browsers can restrict it, and synchronous operations can block the main thread when abused.

- Choose by required lifetime and tab sharing, then keep the value small and non-sensitive. Use IndexedDB or server storage when the data is larger, queried, shared remotely, or authoritative.

sections.title: Origin is not the whole scope
sections.content: localStorage uses origin as its main partition. sessionStorage uses both origin and the top-level browsing context, so two tabs can hold different values for the same key. A newly opened page can initially receive a copy from its opener in some cases, but later changes remain separate.

sections.title: Strings, serialization, and reliability
sections.content: Web Storage stores strings, so objects need explicit serialization and parsing. Missing keys return null, malformed old data can fail JSON parsing, and writes can throw when storage is unavailable or its quota is exceeded. An application should treat stored values as a cache or user preference, validate them after reading, and keep a working in-memory default.

sections.title: Scope and lifetime
sections.content:
| Property | localStorage | sessionStorage |
|---|---|---|
| Data type | String key-value | String key-value |
| Scope | Origin | Origin + top-level tab |
| Reload | Survives | Survives |
| New ordinary tab | Shared for same origin | Separate page session |
| Browser restart | Normally survives | Page session ends |

questions.question: How does the storage event work across browser tabs?
questions.title: The storage event
questions.direct_answer: When one document changes a Web Storage area, other eligible documents receive a storage event with the changed key and old and new values. The window that performed the change does not receive that event.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of same-origin Web Storage notification scope and one-way event delivery.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Waiting for a storage event in the same tab that called setItem(), or treating it as durable messaging.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: localStorage changes reach other same-origin tabs; sessionStorage events remain within the same top-level browsing context, such as eligible iframes.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A storage mutation notifies other eligible documents, not its own window.
The event carries key, oldValue, newValue, url, and storageArea.
localStorage can notify other same-origin tabs.
The event is a state-change signal, not a reliable message queue.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- The `storage` event lets documents learn that another document changed a Web Storage area. It fires on other eligible windows, not on the window that called `setItem`, `removeItem`, or `clear`.

- With localStorage, same-origin pages in other tabs can receive the event. With sessionStorage, delivery stays within the same top-level browsing context, so it may reach a same-origin iframe in the tab but not an unrelated tab.

- For example, when one settings tab stores `theme=dark`, another open same-origin tab can read the event's key and newValue and update its theme. The writing tab should update its own interface directly.

- The event reports a change, but it is not a durable or ordered application message bus. A tab can open after the change, close during delivery, or find that several updates have already happened.

- Listeners should treat storage as the current source, validate the value, and make updates idempotent. BroadcastChannel or a server connection is a clearer fit for richer live communication.

sections.title: Notification follows the stored state
sections.content: The event contains `key`, `oldValue`, `newValue`, the URL that initiated the change, and the affected Storage object. Clearing storage uses null values for the key and value fields. The event does not bubble and cannot be canceled.

sections.title: Synchronize state, not commands
sections.content: A command such as “show toast number 7” loses meaning if it is missed, but state such as “theme is dark” can be read again. That makes storage events appropriate for small cross-tab state refreshes. The listener can re-read the latest value instead of replaying every intermediate event, which also handles several changes arriving close together.

sections.title: Two-tab update
sections.content:
Tab A: localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark')
   ├─ update Tab A UI directly
   └────────────────────────────→ Tab B: `storage` event
                                     key = theme
                                     newValue = dark
                                     update Tab B from validated state
